intercrop_subpractice_raw: 1M:1HB (2005): 1 row of maize + 1 row of haricot bean
intercrop_subpractice: Intercrop (N fixing and Non N fixing)
fert_subpractice_raw: Diammonium phosphate and urea were applied at the rate of 100kg ha−1 at planting and knee height of maize (4–5weeks after planting), respectively.
out_exp_design: Five plants per plot were randomly sampled, dissected and checked for stem borer damage, stem borer life stages and parasitism (5 plants x 3 replications per treatment). In all plots, yield and other data were collected from the central 6 × 6m area of each plot to exclude edge effects. Each treatment was replicated three times in a completely randomized block design.
out_subindicator_description_raw: Borer density per plant. Five plants per plot were randomly sampled, dissected and checked for stem borer damage, stem borer life stages and parasitism. Data on borer density and parasitism were gathered at grain filling and harvest. Pupae were kept in plastic Petri dishes (15mm diameter) until adult borer or parasitoid emergence. Moist tissue papers were placed in the Petri dishes and changed periodically to prevent desiccation of the pupae.

exp_design: Dung beetles were sampled in four habitats between January and June 1995: primary forest (PF), secondary forest (SF), pasture (P) and cropland (C). Four sites were selected for each habitat
subpractice_description_raw: PF: The native primary forest is characterized by arboreal species of Lauraceae, Rubiaceae, Melastomataceae, Palmae, Bombacaceae, Euphorbiaceae and Cesalpinaceae, that have a canopy height of about 30 m, and numerous vines and epiphytes.
land_structure_subpractice_raw: PF: The native primary forest is characterized by arboreal species of Lauraceae, Rubiaceae, Melastomataceae, Palmae, Bombacaceae, Euphorbiaceae and Cesalpinaceae, that have a canopy height of about 30 m, and numerous vines and epiphytes.
out_exp_design: On each site, a transect was established containing eight baited pitfall traps (1000 ml capacity, 13 cm deep, 11 cm diameter) situated 50 m apart. Sampling sites were located one to 10 km apart (Fig. 1). Pitfall traps used to capture specimens were baited with ca. 50 cm³ of fresh human dung, as it has been shown to be a broad-spectrum attractant of Scarabaeinae species. Traps were baited between 06:00 and 08:00 hr, and all specimens were collected after 48 hr. During the first three sampling months, the traps were checked every 12 hr in order to identify each species’ period of daily activity.
product_raw: In a montane region of Colombia, the diversity and composition of the dung beetle (Scarabaeinae) assemblages were sampled and analyzed in natural and anthropogenic habitats: primary forest, secondary forest, pasture and crop-land

site_id01: Sierra de las Minas, Polochic Valley
exp_design: Points were located along approximately 2-km transects which were established as much as possible within a single drainage and elevation zone … Points were located at least 25 m from the edge of the woodlots and 200 m from the nearest point … The distribution of the number of points for each habitat is as follows: sun coffee (28 points in Pueblo Viejo, 82 in Tucurú); Inga (122 Tamahú, 82 Tucurú); Gliricidia (25 Jolomjix, 80 Tucurú); matorral (20 Pueblo Viejo, 57 Tucurú), shade cardamom (55 Pueblo Viejo, 46 Tucurú), forest remnant (50 Tamahú, 21 Tucurú)
time_raw: Most counts in coffee plantations and matorral were surveyed twice: once in period I (January–February 1995) and again in period II (mid-March–mid-April). Forest habitats were surveyed only once during the study
subpractice_description_raw: Inga shade coffee: over 45 species of trees were found in the Inga
agrof_subpractice_raw: Both shade plantation types are characterized by a low (6–8 m) and relatively open (40–50% cover) canopy (Table 1). Gliricidia plantations are strongly dominated (85%) by the most common tree (vs. 61% for Inga) and show considerably lower vertical structural complexity compared to Inga plantations (within-point Coefficient of Variation [CV] of tree height 5 11% versus 20%, respectively). In areas of sun plantations that have trees, the trees are small (5–6 m) and the canopy cover negligible ... Trees are usually trimmed twice each year to maintain a parasol architecture that casts a monolayer of shade (Sanchez Castillo 1994) and to avoid too much humidity, which is believed to promote fungal disease ... In addition to these natural rhythms, shade trees were heavily pruned in approximately half the plantations between the two census periods, substantially reducing shade cover
weed_method_raw: The coffee layer provides few resources for omnivorous or granivorous birds (which dominate matorral) because "weeds" are discouraged through the use of herbicides
chem_subpractice_raw: All of the Guatemalan plantations used insecticides (Siguenza personal communication)
land_structure_subpractice_raw: Inga shade coffee: over 45 species of trees were found in the Inga
out_exp_design: Bird census data are based on fixed radius points counts in a total of 666, 25m fixed radus plots. To avoid basing our analysis on replication over too small an area, we used the mean number of individuals observed over all the points in a single transect
out_subindicator_description_raw: Number of species expected in samples of 400 individuals (based on rarefaction analysis)
extraction_obs: Location is an average between the 4 sites (as measurements don't correspond to one specific site). Buffer is very large because of that reason. Field size given is an average of the 12 plantations studied (range 26-1000 ha). Outcome plot size is the area of each sampling point. Results per system used different numbers of points. Cardamom richness are the only values recorded for Period I instead of Period II as there were only measures for period I

exp_design: Based on aerial photographs from 1996 (and in some cases 1984–1985) we selected all forest patches of more than 1 km2. Of these (approximately 40), we selected 15 areas evenly distributed in the elevational range of 1700–2000 m asl. In a similar manner we selected all agricultural areas of more than 1 km2 from aerial photos from 1967, 1975, and 1984–1985. To be considered an agricultural site, the area had to have been in cultivation on the oldest available aerial photo. On the basis of this initial selection we selected 15 sites that were evenly distributed in the area and in the same elevational range as the forest sites. Finally, we selected all stands (around 20) that appeared to be exotic tree plantations (i.e., dense tree cover in an area that in the oldest aerial photos was treeless). In the field we randomly selected one tree in each of the forest sites in an area that was minimally disturbed by humans (selective logging, beehives, coffee production) and >200 m from the forest edge. In the center of the agricultural sites, we selected a mature shade tree in a home garden with coffee (in one site we found no such home garden, hence n = 14). In the plantations we selected a random tree in the middle of the stand. We selected 7 Cupressus-plantations and six Eucalyptus plantations (n = 13 exotic plantations) to get an even distribution between the two plantation types. (See Supporting Information for a list of the sites and Fig. 1 for the distribution of the sites across the investigated landscape.)

exp_design: Ten rainforest fragments ranging in size from 11 ha to 2,600 ha under varying levels of degradation within the Indira Gandhi Wildlife Sanctuary and private lands of the Valparai plateau, and two shade-coffee plantation sites were sampled for spiders using visual searches along time-constrained belt transects between January and May 2005.
subpractice_description_raw: KO: Korangumudi, highly disturbed rainforest fragments.  which also contained portions of abandoned coffee or cardamom plantations with a mixed canopy of native rainforest trees and planted exotic trees such as Maesopsis emenii and Spathodea campanulata, mid altitude.
agrof_subpractice_raw: KO: Korangumudi, highly disturbed rainforest fragments.  which also contained portions of abandoned coffee or cardamom plantations with a mixed canopy of native rainforest trees and planted exotic trees such as Maesopsis emenii and Spathodea campanulata, mid altitude.
land_structure_subpractice_raw: KO: Korangumudi, highly disturbed rainforest fragments.  which also contained portions of abandoned coffee or cardamom plantations with a mixed canopy of native rainforest trees and planted exotic trees such as Maesopsis emenii and Spathodea campanulata, mid altitude.
out_exp_design: Visual searches were carried out for spiders along belt transects of 2 m width and a maximum searching height of 1.6 m. Each belt transect was at least 30–50 m from the edge to avoid confounding effects due to the edge. The transects were walked as straight as possible and existing paths and trails in the fragments were used most often, and in the coffee sites the rows between the coffee plants were used. Five belt transects were surveyed in each fragment at least once every month between January and May 2005, except in the largest site (IYAK) where seven transects were surveyed, and in MA and AN where four transects were surveyed. The area covered by each transect varied and hence, for each transect, the number of spiders detected on each transect was divided by the area of the transect and multiplied by 100 to obtain spider species density per 100 m2. The values were averaged across the replicates and the standard devi- ation values calculated for each site sampled.
out_subindicator_description_raw: Mean number of species density per 100 m2 of transect area across sites within the treatment. [VISUAL APPROXIMATION from Fig 2a: per-site values read from published graph (+/- 0.5 precision on mean, +/- 0.5 on within-site SD). Paper text confirms overall range 2-3.6 species/100 m2.]

exp_design: Comparison of 5 land-use systems (natural forest, multistrata agroforest, cocoa agroforest, cassava monoculture, weedy grassland) across several villages near Pucallpa city, Peruvian Amazon. Four sampling plots per village (25 x 25 m); each plot sampled six times with monthly repetition (Macuya forest only four times). Insects collected using one Malaise trap, nine pitfall traps in a 5 x 5 m grid, and sweeping net zigzag transects (80 m) per plot, between 6:30-10:30 am, March-August 2009 and February-November 2010. Per Table 1, not all habitats occur in all villages.
time_raw: March to August 2009, and February to November 2010
subpractice_description_raw: primary natural forest (selectively logged 20+ yrs ago; closed canopy; 9 trees/25 m2; 95% ground shade) and ~20 yr old closed-canopy forest in Pimental
agrof_subpractice_raw: Natural forest selectively logged 20+ years, on the edges; trees, palms, shrubs, thick layer of fallen leaves and woody material; Closed canopy; tree density 9 trees/25 m2; 95% ground shade, several natural streams and small ponds of  standing water.
land_structure_subpractice_raw: Natural forest selectively logged 20+ years, on the edges; trees, palms, shrubs, thick layer of fallen leaves and woody material; Closed canopy; tree density 9 trees/25 m2; 95% ground shade, several natural streams and small ponds of  standing water.
out_exp_design: 12 plots of 25 x 25 m sampled (4 per village x 3 villages), plus Macuya forest plots. Each plot sampled with 1 Malaise trap + 9 pitfall traps (5x5 m grid) + sweep net (80 m zigzag transect). Samples collected after 24 h. Insects sorted into morphospecies; Coleoptera, Hymenoptera, Orthoptera, Homoptera and Dictyoptera (Blattodea) retained for analysis.

subpractice_description_raw: In rustic plantations, coffee is grown under the shade of native vegetation, such as Heliocarpus sp., Quercus sartorii, Myrsine coriacea, and Trema micrantha, with some selected shade trees, such as Inga spp. and Citrus spp. The farmers predominantly use alternative management techniques, such as manual weed control and occasional pruning of coffee plants, with no addition of fertilizer
fert_subpractice_raw: These rustic plantations have low management intensity; the farmers predominantly use alternative management techniques, such as manual weed control and occasional pruning of coffee plants, with no addition of fertilizer
weed_method_raw: These rustic plantations have low management intensity; the farmers predominantly use alternative management techniques, such as manual weed control and occasional pruning of coffee plants, with no addition of fertilizer.
chem_subpractice_raw: These rustic plantations have low management intensity; the farmers predominantly use alternative management techniques, such as manual weed control and occasional pruning of coffee plants, with no addition of fertilizer.
out_exp_design:
Ten coffee plants, spaced at least 2 m apart, were chosen from each of the four plantations. To homogenize the sample collection, healthy, mature leaves from north-facing branches growing in the middle of the selected coffee plants were collected. Four coffee leaves from the middle part of the selected branches were collected, stored in a cool box above ice
processed within 48 h
product_raw: We analyzed the diversity and communities of foliar endophytic fungi inhabiting Coffea arabica plants
out_subindicator_description_raw: Mean of EF richness in coffee leaves

weed_method_raw: Weeding was done manually once to help seedling establishment and all weeds were incorporated into the soil.
out_exp_design: Soil samples were collected using a steel monolith sampler (25 ? 25 ? 25 cm) placed over a randomly selected spot and driven into the soil to ground level using a metallic mallet. Three monoliths (within 3â€“5 m of each other) were taken from each of the replicate plots bringing the total number of sampling units per treatment to nine. The soil was removed from the sampler, macrofauna were hand-sorted and separated into higher taxa (family and order). In some taxa such as Coleoptera, where both larvae and adults were encountered, adults Ã¾ larvae were recorded as total beetles. Samples were taken on 4 different occasions, but results in this database are for each occasion separately so n=9

The soil was removed from the sampler, macrofauna were hand-sorted and separated into higher taxa (family and order). In some taxa such as Coleoptera, where both larvae and adults were encountered, adults Ã¾ larvae were recorded as total beetles. time_raw: Two experiments were carried out between March and December 1998
subpractice_description_raw: Monocrop Bean (Diversity study, Imidacloprid): Monocrop plots consisted of eight rows of bean
varietal_crop_subpractice_raw: The bean variety used was ICTA-Santa Gertudis, a cultivar developed and promoted by ICTA as resistant to bean golden mosaic
intercrop_subpractice_raw: Monocrop Bean (Diversity study, Imidacloprid): Monocrop plots consisted of eight rows of bean
fert_subpractice_raw: Application of fertilizer, weeding, and all other aspects of plot management were carried out manually. Coop.,  Guipuzcoa, Spain).
weed_method_raw: Application of fertilizer, weeding, and all other aspects of plot management were carried out manually. Crops were fertilized according to local recommendations (ICTA 1993, Superb 1997). Fungicides and pesticides were applied with a 16-liter Matabi  “Super 16” backpack sprayer (Goizper S. Coop.,  Guipuzcoa, Spain).
chem_subpractice_raw: Imidacloprid (ConÞdor 70 WG; Bayer AG) was prepared at a rate of 0.73 g/liter of water. Approximately 0.01 liters (10 cc) of this mixture (7.3 mg imidacloprid) was applied to the base of each bean plant receiving the imidacloprid treatment. Imidacloprid was applied to bean at emergence, 1 wk after emergence, and 3 wk after emergence. Imidacloprid is not registered for bean, and was included for comparison only.
irrig_subpractice_raw: Water from a furrow irrigation system was made available to the station every 6 d for 3 d during the dry season and upon request during the rainy season.
out_exp_design: Bean plants were sampled on six occasions: 17 April (1 wk after emergence), 25 April, 3 May, 12 May, 19 May, and 17 June. The sample unit on 17 April, 25 April, 3 May, and 19 May (samples 1Ð3 and 5) was a 3.35-cm2 disc removed with a cork borer from upper and lower stratum leaves (McAuslane et al. 1995). The disc was removed from the underside of the central leaßet to the right of the mid-vein. Five plants per plot were sampled on these dates. The average of the two discs was used in treatment analysis. On 12 May and 17 June (samples 4 and 6), one whole plant per subplot replicate was sampled.
out_subindicator_description_raw: Densities of whitefly nymphs in bean foliage
extraction_obs: While the plot size is not stated explicitly, Diversity Study Plot Size (153 m²): The paper states that "Whole plots contained nine rows, 17 m in length" and that the "Space between rows was 1.0 m". Multiplying the 9-meter width (9 rows × 1.0 m) by the 17-meter length results in 153 m². Mosaic Study Plot Size (64 m²): For this study, the paper describes that "Intercrop plots consisted of eight rows" and "Rows were 8 m in length and between-row spacing was 1.0 m". Multiplying the 8-meter width (8 rows × 1.0 m) by the 8-meter length results in 64 m². The density for each crop was then derived by determining the total number of plants intended for each plot based on the intra-row spacing for each crop as reported in each treatment, and dividing that total by the plot area. The amount of pesticide imidacloprid per plant is 7.3 mg per plant (noted in pp. 91)

exp_design: The experiment was set-up as a randomized block design with four treatments and four replicates of each treatment. Rice was rotated with maize and mungbean in different combinations. Each year, the three cropping periods were November–February (only rice crop in all treatments), March–June (rotation crops) and July–October (rice or maize crops) with four treatments: (1) rice–rice–rice (RRR) as control, (2) rice–maize–rice (RMR), (3) rice–mungbeanmaize (RMgM), and (4) rice–mungbean–rice (RMgR). These crop rotation treatments were repeated yearly from 2001 to 2008.
